rows.evidence: Q1: Case study section, Figures 2-4 and Table 3 - the authors compute their own dekadal anomaly percentiles and drought onset/duration/severity statistics for the 2014 Senegal drought from CHIRPS, H SAF, ESA CCI, SWI, NDVI and VODCA datasets (2007-2018), reporting that the datasets correspond well and detect the drought.
rows.notes: The paper is labelled a review; only the Senegal case study is the authors' own analysis (Q1 marked yes on that basis, with doubt). The case study shows that microwave-based soil moisture and VOD anomalies capture the spatio-temporal development of the 2014 drought; it does not measure crop development, crop yield or any crop-production outcome (yield deficits are only cited from external reports), nor does it evaluate microwave SM as an aid to crop development. It supports only the precondition (soil moisture/drought assessment) of the claimed crop-production benefit.

rows.evidence: Q1: Case study section, Figures 2-4 and Table 3 - own anomaly-percentile analysis of satellite rainfall, soil moisture and vegetation datasets over Senegal for the 2014 drought.
rows.notes: The study's own result concerns drought detection (onset, duration, severity) with microwave soil moisture and vegetation products over rainfed Senegal. It contains no irrigation-scheduling or water-conservation result; irrigation is mentioned only as a likely reason why the area near the Senegal river appeared less drought-affected. Soil moisture assessment is at most a precondition for irrigation scheduling optimisation.

notes: Document is a review paper (Frontiers in Water, TYPE Review) with an embedded Senegal case study based on the authors' own processing of existing satellite datasets; no field measurements, crop yield data or irrigation trials are reported. Full text appears complete. Q1 could reasonably be judged 'no' if the case study is not considered primary data; the outcome for Q2-Q9 is 'no' either way.
